summary: Introduces a Path Segment Identifier for Segment Routing over MPLS. Because a list of segments may overlap with another path, an egress node cannot tell which path a packet took. A path identifier lets the egress recognize the path, which helps uses such as performance measurement and 1+1 path protection.

eli5.summary: Two buses may share many of the same stops, so a stop alone can't tell you which bus you rode. This adds a ticket number so the last stop knows exactly which route a packet took.

questions: what is a path segment identifier
what is a psid in sr-mpls
where is the psid placed in the mpls label stack
subtitle: A single extra MPLS label that tells the last router on a Segment Routing path which path a packet took.

tldr.problem: In SR-MPLS the labels are swapped or popped along the way, so by the time a packet reaches the egress node little or nothing of the label stack is left to show which SR path it followed.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress node adds a Path Segment Identifier (PSID), one label taken from the egress node's Segment Routing Local Block, right after the last label of the path. The egress node pops it and can use it to recognize the path.
tldr.outcome: Egress nodes can tell paths apart, which is a prerequisite for performance measurement, bidirectional paths and 1+1 path protection. It costs extra processing at the egress and per-path state there.

facts.label: Position
facts.value: Immediately after the last label of the SR path

today: RFC 9545 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2024, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Signaling of PSIDs and the detailed solutions for the use cases are left to other documents.

sections.title: Why Paths Need an Identifier
sections.content:
In Segment Routing (SR), a source node steers a packet by prepending a list of instructions called segments. With the MPLS data plane, that list is a stack of MPLS labels. As the packet moves, labels are swapped or popped, so when it reaches the egress node, no label or only the last label may be left.

That means the egress node cannot use the label stack to learn which SR path the packet followed. A subset of segments cannot tell two paths apart either, because paths can be partly congruent. Yet several use cases need that knowledge: performance measurement, bidirectional paths and end-to-end 1+1 path protection.

RFC 9545 therefore defines a new segment type, the Path Segment, that uniquely identifies an SR path at its egress node. Using it is optional for the egress node (MAY). The RFC notes that per-path state must then be kept at the egress node, whereas normally only the ingress node keeps it.
sections.eli5: When a parcel arrives at the last depot, the shipping labels have been peeled off along the way. The depot cannot tell which route it came by, so we add one more sticker that names the route.

sections.title: The Path Segment and the PSID
sections.content:
A Path Segment is a local segment that identifies an SR path on the egress node. Its identifier, the PSID, is a single label assigned from the Segment Routing Local Block (SRLB) of the egress node.

A PSID normally identifies one segment list. One PSID can also identify several segment lists, for example some or all segment lists of a candidate path or SR policy, if an operator wants to aggregate them.

How the PSID is signaled between the egress node, the ingress node and possibly a central controller is out of scope for this document.
sections.eli5: Each last stop hands out its own numbered tickets, and a ticket only means something at that stop. One ticket can even cover several similar routes if the bus company wants.

sections.title: Where the PSID Goes in the Label Stack
sections.content:
The ingress node inserts the PSID so that it MUST immediately follow the last label of the SR path, meaning after the adjacency, node or prefix segment that points to the egress node. As a result the PSID is never the top label at an intermediate node, though it can be the top label on the penultimate node.

  • The TTL of the label stack entry can be any value except 0.
  • If the PSID is the bottom label, the S bit MUST be set; otherwise the S bit MUST be 0.
  • The egress node MUST pop the PSID and MAY use it for further processing, such as triggering packet counting or timestamping when performance measurement is on.

Reading the extra label may affect forwarding performance. Behavior when an explicit null label directly precedes the PSID is undefined here. The Maximum SID Depth (MSD) that a node can impose counts the PSID among the total MPLS labels. If a Generic Associated Channel Label is used for OAM, the Associated Channel Header still comes right after the bottom of the stack.
sections.eli5: The extra ticket goes at the very end of the list of directions, just before the parcel itself. Stops in the middle never see it on top, and the last stop tears it off.

sections.title: Equal-Cost Multipath Considerations
sections.content:
An Entropy Label (EL) and its indicator, if used, sit before the tunnel label, so they do not interfere with the PSID below them.

With ECMP, SR packets may be forwarded over several paths. The segment list then does not directly reflect the actual forwarding path, so a PSID identifies the segment list, not the physical path taken.

As with a Synonymous Flow Label, adding a PSID to an existing flow may make that flow take a different path under ECMP, which can invalidate uses such as performance measurement. The RFC says the considerations in Section 5 of RFC 8957 therefore also apply to PSIDs.
sections.eli5: If a road splits into several equal lanes, your ticket names the route you planned, not necessarily the lane you drove in. Adding a ticket can even change which lane the packet gets sent down.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
This section is informative; detailed solutions may appear in other documents.

Performance measurement. Measuring points such as the ingress and egress nodes, or a controller, can use the PSID to match packet counts and timestamps for one SR path, and so calculate loss and delay end to end. The PSID can also support active measurement with probes, in situ OAM data (RFC 9197) and in-band performance measurement.

Bidirectional paths. An SR path is unidirectional, so a bidirectional path can bind two unidirectional ones. PSIDs identify and correlate the traffic of the two directions at both ends. How to build such paths is out of scope.

1+1 path protection. In the Live-Live case the egress node must know which paths are primary and secondary, so it can forward primary packets and discard the others. This needs a path identifier unique at the egress node, which can be the Path Segment label it allocated.
sections.eli5: The ticket number lets both ends of a trip count parcels and compare notes, pair a trip there with a trip back, and spot which of two copies sent by different routes to keep.

sections.title: Nesting of PSIDs
sections.content:
A Binding SID (BSID) can compress a SID list by splitting an end-to-end path in a trusted domain into sub-paths, each identified by a BSID. A BSID and a PSID can be combined to monitor both sub-paths and the whole path.

The RFC's reference model has an end-to-end path from A to D across Access, Aggregation and Core subdomains, made of sub-paths A to B, B to C and C to D. The SID list of a sub-path is <SID1, SID2, ..., SIDn, s-PSID>, and the SID list of the end-to-end path is <BSID1, BSID2, ..., BSIDn, e-PSID>. Each sub-path has a BSID and an s-PSID, and the e-PSID stays at the bottom of the stack along the whole way.
sections.eli5: A long trip can be split into legs, each with its own ticket, while one big ticket for the whole trip stays with you from start to finish.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A PSID is a local label like a VPN label, and its processing follows the same logic as the existing MPLS data plane. Only the egress and ingress nodes of the path learn it; intermediate nodes do not.

A PSID is used inside an SR-MPLS trusted domain and must not leak outside it, so the RFC says it introduces no new threats compared with current SR-MPLS. Domain boundary routers MUST filter external traffic aimed at a label of a segment inside the domain, and that applies to a PSID too. The other considerations in Section 8.1 of RFC 8402 also apply.

Distributing a PSID from egress to ingress happens inside the trusted domain and is out of scope. This document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The ticket numbers are internal to the bus company, so the gates at the edge must turn away outsiders who try to use them.
